694.title: Sulayman's du'a
694.hook: inspire me to be grateful, and to do good that pleases You (27:19)
694.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize the du'a of 27:19, rabbi awzi'ni an ashkura ni'mataka, and say it in moments of success or gratitude; the similar words of 46:15 are often taught as a du'a for parents and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zakariyya in the sanctuary, and your line: don't leave me alone. Did your message reach someone who needed it? Today, a king with everything, stopped in his tracks by an ant. Day six hundred ninety-four.

An army on the march: people, jinn and birds, the Qur'an says, all in their ranks, and at the front a king, Sulayman, the one the Bible calls Solomon. They come to a valley full of ants. And one ant calls out to the others: get into your homes, or Sulayman and his soldiers will crush you without even noticing. Surah twenty-seven says Sulayman heard her. He had been taught the speech of birds, the surah says, and here he understands an ant. And the most powerful man in the story stops, and smiles.
screen: `AN ARMY IN THE VALLEY OF THE ANTS.`

segments.voice: What he does next is surah twenty-seven, verse nineteen. He smiled, laughing at her words, and prayed. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord, arouse me to be thankful for Thy favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents, and to do good that shall be pleasing unto Thee." The word Pickthall renders arouse me is awzi'ni. Translators give it as inspire me, or keep me devoted, or urge me on. The point is the same: Sulayman doesn't trust himself to stay grateful on his own. He asks to be kept at it. Think of what he has. A kingdom, an army, a gift for languages no one else has. And the moment that gift shows him something, a tiny creature worried about her family, his first reaction isn't pride. It's thanks, and a request for help to keep thanking. Notice too who he includes: me and my parents. The gift that let him hear an ant didn't start with him. Later in the same surah, when a throne is brought to him in the blink of an eye, he says, in effect, this is from my Lord's bounty, to test me whether I give thanks or turn ungrateful. So for Sulayman, a skill is also a question. One more detail: nearly the same words come back in surah forty-six, in the mouth of an ordinary person who reaches forty years old. The king's prayer turns out to be a prayer for anyone who has been given anything.
screen: `AWZI'NI: KEEP ME AT IT, INSPIRE ME.`

segments.voice: The practice: give thanks for one skill. Sit, and breathe. Pick one thing you can do: cook a dish without a recipe, calm a crying baby, fix a sink, make a stranger laugh, read this sentence. Now trace it back. Who taught you, or who gave you the time to learn it? A parent, a teacher, a coworker who was patient once. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the skill and for the people behind it, in your own words or with Sulayman's. If you don't, simply hold the skill and the people with it, gratefully. The bell holds the time.
Sulayman's du'a. A king who heard an ant, smiled, and asked to be kept grateful, for himself and for his parents, and to do good that pleases Allah. Today's word.
Your line: inspire me to be grateful. Today, when someone praises something you do well, pass the praise along: name one person who taught you. Day six hundred ninety-four.

pairs: warned the others to go home
inspire me, keep me at it

he smiled, laughed, and prayed to be kept grateful.

695.title: The believers' du'a
695.hook: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve, and give us mercy from You (3:8)
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book read through
695.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize 3:8, rabbana la tuzigh qulubana, and say it after the daily prayers or in personal du'a, alongside the Prophet's own prayer, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sulayman and the ant, and your line: inspire me to be grateful. Did you pass some praise along to the person who taught you? Today, the last du'a of this run, and the first spoken not by a prophet but by a whole group of believers. Day six hundred ninety-five.

Umm Salamah, one of the wives of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, noticed something. A prayer he said more than any other, she reported, was this: O turner of hearts, keep my heart firm on Your religion. She asked him why that one, so often. He answered, in the hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, that every human heart lies between two of the fingers of Allah, and He turns it as He wills. The one person, many Muslims would say, with the least reason to worry about his heart, asked most often for it to be kept.

He was not the first to ask this. The Qur'an puts the same request in the mouths of a whole group. Surah three, verse seven, talks about the book itself: some verses are clear and plain, others are open to more than one reading. Some people chase the unclear ones to stir up trouble, it says. But those firmly grounded in knowledge say: we believe in it, it is all from our Lord. And then, verse eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us, and bestow upon us mercy from Thy Presence. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Bestower." Look at who is praying. Not beginners. The people the verse calls firm in knowledge, the ones who have studied the hard parts. And look at the phrase after Thou hast guided us. This isn't a prayer to find the way. It's a prayer not to lose it. Guidance, in this verse, is not a trophy you keep on a shelf. It can slip. The Arabic word for heart, qalb, comes from a root about turning over, and the scholars noticed the fit: a heart is the thing that turns. So the people who know the most ask, like the Prophet did, to be kept. This whole week has been prophets' du'as: Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Sulayman. Today's belongs to everyone who has been guided at all.
screen: `THE FIRMLY GROUNDED SAY: ALL FROM OUR LORD.`
`DON'T LET OUR HEARTS STRAY, AFTER GUIDANCE.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it after prayer. Sit, and feel your heart beating, steady, without your help. If you pray, you can say the believers' words, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after You have guided us, and give us mercy from You. Many Muslims say it after the daily prayer; you can begin with this sit. If you don't pray, think of one thing you hold dear that you'd hate to drift from, and simply hold it while the heart keeps time. The bell holds the time.
The believers' du'a. Our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after guidance, and give us mercy from You. Said by those firm in knowledge, and asked for most by the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: keep my heart. Today, pick one good habit you already have and give it a small guard: set the reminder, lay out the mat, put the book where you'll see it. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the book read through
696.hook: from the Opening to the thirtieth part, the whole Qur'an has now been heard once
696.howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a reading of the whole Qur'an, a khatm, especially during Ramadan, often closing with a gathering and du'a, and in many communities a new reading begins at once with the Fatiha and the opening of al-Baqarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the believers' du'a, and your line: keep my heart. Did you put a small guard around one good habit? Today, the last day of year two, and a whole book behind you. Day six hundred ninety-six.

On the first day of this year, your line was: from the opening, onward. You were asked to choose a daily reading time. Since then this path has walked from surah one, the Fatiha, through the Cow and the Family of Imran, past Yusuf and Maryam and the Cave, through the Ant and the Stories, all the way to surah seventy-seven. Year one had already carried the last part, the thirtieth, from seventy-eight to the end. Put the two years together, and something has happened quietly.

Every one of the hundred and fourteen surahs has now been heard on this path at least once. Let's be honest about what that means. The short surahs came whole. The long ones came by theme, a passage and an idea at a time, not every verse read aloud. So this is a first hearing, not a full recitation. But it has a shape Muslims know well. Finishing the Qur'an from beginning to end is called a khatm, a sealing or completing, and it has a long history. A hadith in al-Bukhari says the angel Jibril went over the Qur'an with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. Many Muslims aim for a khatm each Ramadan; some families and mosques gather to hear its final surahs together and make du'a. And in many communities, the moment one reading ends, the next one begins: back to the Fatiha, and the first lines of the Cow. The book has no last page, only a place where you turn around. The year was built in five blocks: the Opening and the long Medinan surahs; prophets, parables and light; a holy-days interlude; the middle of the book; and then the run toward the thirtieth part. The last month gathered it all: the prophets named, the women remembered, justice, mercy, the earth, and this past week, the prophets' own du'as. Pickthall's translation of the Fatiha opens: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." That is where the reading began. It is also where the next one starts.
screen: `A FIRST HEARING, NOT A FULL RECITATION.`

segments.voice: The practice: the Fatiha, and your carried verse. Sit, and let your breath slow. If you pray, recite the Fatiha, in Arabic if you know it, or hear its meaning in English, line by line. Then bring back one verse from this year that stayed with you. Maybe a healing and a mercy. Maybe I was wrong. Maybe no compulsion. Say it once, or simply hold it. If you don't pray, just let one line from the year come back to you, and notice why it was that one that stayed. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. From the Fatiha to surah seventy-seven, joined to last year's thirtieth part: every surah, heard once. A khatm, and a door back to the beginning. Today's word.

Your line: the whole book, heard once. Today, write down the one verse you're carrying out of this year, and put it where next year will find it. Tomorrow, year three: the people who carried this book. Day six hundred ninety-six.
